newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: North Korea said to stage public executions.
newsitem.headline: North Korea said to stage public executions.

text.p: Amnesty International said on Thursday it had good evidence that communist North Korea had staged many public executions over the past 30 years and that they may be continuing in the late 1990s.

In a report made available in Geneva, the London-based organisation said it also believed that the death penalty in general was much more widely used for criminal and perhaps political offences than the North Korean authorities admit.
"Converging testimonies from a variety of unconnected witnesses indicate that public executions have been carried out...for many years, that they have continued into the 1990s," the report said.

Amnesty cited accounts from North Korean citizens outside the country of shootings and hangings since 1970 in several areas of the reclusive state which were announced in advance and often attended by children as well as adults.
These accounts led it to fear that despite official denials public executions, banned under international conventions, "may still take place."

None of these witnesses had been interviewed in South Korea and no information had been used from any government other than that of North Korea, Amnesty said -- clearly aiming to avert suggestions it might have used suspect sources.

Although the last execution mentioned by the witnesses was in 1992, of a man accused of murder, Amnesty said because it was not allowed to make on-the-spot checks inside the country information often took a long time to gather.

The organisation, which makes frequent submissions to United Nations' human rights bodies sitting in Geneva, sent a mission to Pyongyang in 1995 and the report noted that North Korea says the death penalty is only rarely used.

It was difficult to make any reliable estimate of the total, it added, but the fact that almost all the North Koreans it interviewed abroad had witnessed death sentences being carried out suggested it was a regular occurrence.
Amnesty said it had been told of executions on river banks, on athletics grounds and in sports stadiums attended by crowds ranging from a few hundred up to several thousand.
At least two were staged in or on the edge of Pyongyang, the capital, according to the eyewitness accounts.

The report said in the 16 cases on which it had testimony, covering a total of 24 executions, the accusations ranged from stealing rice -- for which two brothers went to their deaths in the early 1980s -- to murder and rape.

None of the the witnesses, who declined to allow their names to be cited for fear of reprisals against relatives still in the country, recounted executions for political motives, according to the report.

But Amnesty noted that under the current North Korean criminal code the death penalty is mandatory for activities "in collusion with imperialists" and aimed at "suppressing the national liberation struggle."
Other offences that automatically bring death are actions against "the revolutionary struggle for reunification and independence" and "acts of betraying the Nation to imperialists," the report said.
